pitch: How the modern world was assembled, by force and by accident.
digest: Krall argues that the modern world order was produced by a small number of decisions taken for immediate reasons — the Westphalian settlement, the balance of power, the division of the world into economic and political blocs — and that none of them was intended to produce the system that resulted. The chapters on the Peace of Westphalia and on the economic orders are the strongest, and his case that the system's stability comes from an unresolved contradiction is a serious one. It is written by a political scientist and argues with other political scientists rather than with popular history.

title: The Age of the Revolution
author: Timothy G. Blanning
pitch: The 1770–1848 period treated as one long upheaval.
digest: Blanning treats the half-century from the American Revolution to the European revolutions of 1848 as a single connected process, which is a genuinely useful framing and mostly works. The chapters on the French Revolution's second phase and on the effect of industrialisation on political consciousness are the strongest. He is unusually attentive to demography and economics for a narrative historian. The conclusion, that this period created the political questions we are still arguing about, is the argument the book is making and it is well supported.

title: The Last Kingdom
author: Bernard Cornwell
pitch: Narrative history as a way of making the period legible.
digest: Cornwell writes history through invented protagonists, which critics have dismissed and readers have consumed by the shelf. The technique works because he is a serious researcher first, and the notes section documents the archaeology he has used. The chapters on the formation of the Danelaw and on the naval technology that made the raids possible are the best of the fiction-adjacent scholarship. This entry sits on the modern shelf because it is still in copyright, but the Anglo-Saxon and Norse material it draws on is in the free part of this library.

title: The Habsburg Empire
author: A. J. P. Taylor
pitch: A multi-national empire held together by a shared dynasty.
digest: Taylor's history of the Habsburgs is an argument that the empire's coherence came from the dynasty rather than from any idea, language or nationality, and that this made it formidable and structurally fragile at the same time. His writing is sceptical in a way that has not dated well and his judgements about individuals are often unfair. The chapters on the relationship with the Ottomans and on the eighteenth-century reforms are the best. It is now read as a period piece as much as a history, which is itself instructive.

title: The Terror: The French Revolution
author: Simon Schama
pitch: The French Revolution as an orgy of killing.
digest: Schama's thesis — that the Terror was not an unavoidable response to circumstance but the pursuit of an ideological objective by a determined faction — is bold and has been heavily contested, partly because it is sympathetic to figures like Foscari whom historians have generally treated differently. He writes about violence better than anyone. As an argument it is now generally rejected, but the descriptive power of the chapters on the guillotine and on the psychology of the revolutionaries has made it permanently readable. The book is best taken as an argument to argue with.

title: The Anarchy
author: William Dalrymple
pitch: The East India Company, and how private profit conquered a subcontinent.
digest: Dalrymple tells the story of the East India Company as the founding institution of British empire, making the case that the conquest of India was the work of a private corporation with its own army, its own diplomacy and no effective oversight. The chapters on Plassey and Buxar and on the Company's army are the core, and he documents the famines and the revenue systems that followed. It is a popular history and a partisan one, and has been criticised for treating eighteenth-century India as merely a backdrop to a British story. The decisive battles are covered in the free military histories on this site.

title: The Republic of Letters
author: Antoine Lilti
pitch: How the Enlightenment actually ran as an institution.
digest: Lilti's account of the Republic of Letters is a history of an institution rather than of a movement, and it shows the correspondence networks, the salons, the patronage, and the reputation economy that made intellectual life possible. The chapters on what made a philosopher a celebrity and on how disagreement was policed within the republic are the strongest. It revises the standard picture of the Enlightenment as a coherent programme in favour of something messier and more interesting. Dense and sociological, and much better than the alternative.

title: The Great Divergence
author: Kenneth Pomeranz
pitch: Why Europe and China diverged, in energy and ecology.
digest: Pomeranz's central argument is that the Industrial Revolution was made possible by coal — specifically by the coal deposits of Britain and the coal-burning of the North China plain — and that the relevant comparison is not Britain and China but the coal-rich and coal-poor parts of each. He builds this on two paired regions with comparable land ratios, land productivity and living standards in 1800. The chapters on the ghost acreage argument and on New World land are the strongest. The book has been challenged on the representativeness of his two regions and has taken a generation of refinement.

title: The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy
author: Jacob Burckhardt
pitch: The founding claim that the Renaissance invented modernity.
digest: Burckhardt's thesis is that the Italian Renaissance marked a genuine break — the discovery of the world and of the individual — and it founded an entire genre of European cultural history. He is wrong in important ways: the break is far less clean, and the most important elements of the Renaissance were reviving antiquity rather than inventing anything. It is also the source of every claim about Michelangelo, Leonardo and the 'men of the Renaissance' that we now repeat. It has been superseded and it is still necessary, which is a remarkable combination for a book.

title: The Sleepwalkers
author: Christopher Clark
pitch: The First World War as a catastrophe nobody chose.
digest: Clark's revisionist account argues that the war of 1914 was not the product of any government's deliberate plan but of a series of decisions each of which seemed reasonable to those making it. The chapters on July 1914 and on the Balkans are the most persuasive part of the case. He is criticised for understating the agency of German decision-makers, and the criticism has force, but the reframing has done real work in the field. It is a long book and the two essays on the war's memory and meaning are the most striking.

title: The Storm of War
author: Antony Beevor
pitch: The Second World War told from the soldiers' side of the line.
digest: Beevor's account begins in 1939 and follows the war from the German perspective for most of its length, which produces an unusually convincing explanation of how the German army fought itself into a corner. The chapters on the Ardennes and on the Eastern Front are the best. He is very good on the institutional failures that produced operational stupidity and very good on the experience of ordinary soldiers on both sides. It is a large book and better for its detail than its analysis, which is quite explicitly episodic.

title: Man's Search for Meaning (revisited)
author: Viktor E. Frankl
pitch: Already on the modern shelf; here for the method behind it.
digest: Frankl's logotherapy grew directly out of his observation that the prisoners who survived were not the youngest or the healthiest but those with something still to complete. The method's central move is to ask what a person is called to do rather than what they want, on the reasoning that meaning is available even when everything else has been taken away. The book's first half is an autobiography written with unusual restraint and the second is a short theoretical exposition. The scientific status of logotherapy has never been strong, but the argument about attention as the remaining freedom is one of the few things everyone in the prison agreed on.

title: Educated
author: Tara Westover
pitch: A life in survivalist Utah, and the cost of leaving it.
digest: Westover's memoir describes growing up in a family that had no birth certificates, no records and no contact with the state, and her eventual discovery that what she had been told about the world was a managed construction. The most striking material is not the abuse but the epistemology — what it does to a mind to grow up inside an account of reality that cannot be checked. Her account of the last piece of coal and the reconciliation with her family is handled with remarkable restraint. It has been criticised for the unresolved ambiguity at the end, which many readers find honest and others find evasive.

title: Hillbilly Elegy
author: J. D. Vance
pitch: Poverty, family loyalty, and a judgement about what to do about it.
digest: Vance's memoir of a Kentucky family on welfare is a detailed account of what makes leaving difficult, and he is admirably unsentimental about the relatives whose actions cost his mother money. The chapter on his grandmother is among the most moving things written about the economics of dependency. What the book has attracted is the argument over its conclusions, since the question it raises — whether individual escape stories generalise to a policy answer — is genuinely hard and the book is not interested in it. The medical details are lurid in a way that has been fairly criticised.

title: Just Kids
author: Patti Smith
pitch: The pre-punk years, written by the person who was there.
digest: Smith's memoir of her late teens and twenties in New York with Robert Mapplethorpe is a book about an artistic friendship rather than a rise to fame, and the early chapters about babysitting for a photographer and selling art on the street have more life in them than any account of the music business. The later years overlap with her arrival and it gets harder. She is unsentimental about her own ambitions and about the sex and drugs of the period. It is one of the best books about how a person is formed by a group of friends.

title: Boy, Erased
author: Garrard Conley
pitch: A memoir of conversion therapy, and what it took to undo.
digest: Conley's memoir describes being sent to conversion therapy as a teenager in a small Arkansas town, and it is far more specific and less polemical than most books about this subject. He is careful to distinguish between the practice being illegal, harmful and ineffective, and to say that many people in it were earnest. The chapters on his parents — how they came to send him, and the decades of subsequent relationship — are the most difficult material and the most valuable. The account of his later work on LGBTQ health in Appalachia avoids the redemption arc that memoirs of this kind usually insist on.

title: The Year of Magical Thinking
author: Joan Didion
pitch: Grief rendered in the clearest prose in English.
digest: Didion's account of the year after her husband's death begins with an inventory of what her body still does, which is the most accurate description of bereavement ever written. She has an unusual and slightly unnerving talent for stating her own selfishness plainly, and she is explicit about how much of her account is really an account of her marriage. The chapters on the year afterwards and on the imagined hospital room are the ones that stay with you. It is not a book about finding meaning and it is better for that.

title: The Diary of a Young Girl
author: Etty Hillesum
pitch: A diarist in Amsterdam, 1940–1942, and what it cost to write.
digest: Hillesum kept a diary through the occupation of Amsterdam, the restrictions on Jews, and the separation from her lover who was sent to a camp. The final entries are almost unbearably restrained in a way that makes them worse, since they show her processing the information she has. The theological passages are not piety but an attempt to construct a response before one is available. It has been frequently misdescribed as a book about maintaining hope in the Holocaust, and Hillesum, who was killed at Auschwitz, wrote no such thing. The prose is the point.

title: A Rumor of War
author: Philip Caputo
pitch: The first week of the Vietnam War, by a marine who was there.
digest: Caputo's memoir covers the seven days his unit spent in a firefight that killed most of the men in it, and its real achievement is refusing the standard war memoir arc of naive boy to sceptical man. He is angry, confused, and undecided for most of it. The chapter on how the news of the engagement was received in America is the one that has aged most, since the shift in public attitudes he describes has continued in a direction he did not predict. It remains the most honest account of what combat does to perception.

title: H Is for Hawk
author: Helen Macdonald
pitch: Grief, a hawk, and a training manual from 1930s Britain.
digest: Macdonald's friend died in an accident and she trained a goshawk, and the book is the space between those two facts. She uses the historical falconry literature to make the present grief legible and to examine the deep strangeness of training an animal that could kill her. The chapters on the training itself are precise and unsentimental and were written with a professional falconer's help, and the chapter on fatherhood is the one that will affect most readers most. It is a genuine literary achievement and the oddest memoir in English.

title: The Diary of Anne Frank
author: Anne Frank
pitch: Two years in hiding, written by a teenager who knew how it ended.
digest: Frank's diary is read as a document of the Holocaust and it is a better book than that framing suggests, because it is a teenager's diary about a teenager's social life with a war running underneath it. The passages on her arguments with her father, on school, on being bored, and on her writing are the ones that make people uncomfortable, because the banality is the point. The redacted passages, restored in later editions, remove most of the coyness in earlier versions and add the sexuality her editors had cut. It is available free in this library in English translation.

title: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
author: Malcolm X
pitch: A conversion narrative told by the person it happened to.
digest: Malcolm X's autobiography, written with Alex Haley, follows him from a childhood in Omaha to prison, to Nation of Islam, to Mecca and a break with it. The transformation chapter, where he discovers that the Muslims in Mecca were not what he had been told, is the most consequential part and it reorganises everything after it. The early chapters on his mother and on the Detroit streets are the most vivid. It has been disputed on grounds of the collaboration, and the handwriting question is real, but it is one of the few genuinely revealing conversion narratives.

title: My Life on the Road
author: Gloria Steinem
pitch: A life in journalism as a way of taking power apart.
digest: Steinem's memoir is organised around undercover assignments rather than chronology, and the best chapters are the ones where she describes entering a world as a different person and then working out what she did to people in it. The accounts of her most contested writing are unusually honest about the harm it caused to people she described. It is a long book and the feminist movement chapters are thinner than the reporting ones, but the discipline she imposes on her own account is what makes it worth reading now.

title: The Woman Warrior
author: Maxine Hong Kingston
pitch: Memory, migration and the unreliable boundary between them.
digest: Kingston's first book mixes her mother's stories, her own childhood in the United States, the myths she was told about China, and the fantasy of the White Jade Princess, and refuses to resolve which is which. Whether it is autobiography, fiction or criticism is the question the book is built on. The later sections on her grandmother's silences and on her own writing are the strongest. It is one of the books that made memoir into something structurally unstable, and it is difficult to categorise in a way that does not damage it.

title: Man Without a Country
author: Kurt Vonnegut
pitch: A short autobiography told entirely through other people.
digest: Vonnegut recounts his life by quoting his own earlier work and the accounts of people who knew him, with a short original chapter between each, on the premise that this is a memoir in the post-war sense: the narrator is a character. It is very funny and it is also a genuine account of a man who found a way to speak about the bombing of Dresden in a form his readers would accept. It is the best short thing he wrote, and it lasts about an hour.

title: Life of Pi
author: Yann Martel
pitch: A boy, a tiger, and the argument about whether story is allowed to save you.
digest: Pi's account of surviving a shipwreck ends with him explaining that two lifeboats and 450 days with a tiger cannot be true, so he offers three versions, the first of which ends in despair and the third in which he is saved. The novel is very good at evoking hunger and religious argument, and it is most interesting as a parable about whether fiction is permissible in the face of fact. Its reputation has fallen somewhat since it won the Booker and risen again as a film, and the case it makes is genuinely harder to state than its detractors assume. It is in copyright here; the older seafaring and survival material in the free library covers the same ground.

title: The Road
author: Cormac McCarthy
pitch: Two people crossing a country, and whether they ever get there.
digest: McCarthy's novel is almost entirely dialogue and description, with almost no interiority, and the effect is a father and son moving south through a burnt landscape toward an outcome the book declines to confirm. The prose has been praised for its purity and attacked for being a style that could be produced by a rule, and both are fair. What is not in dispute is that it is genuinely moving, and that the absence of consolation is doing the work. The historical sources McCarthy used on how people actually prepared for and survived the collapse are printed at the end and are as interesting as the novel.

title: The Constant Gardener
author: John le Carré
pitch: A murder in Kenya that is really about what foreign aid is.
digest: Le Carré wrote this at the end of his career and it shows in its compressed length and its sharpness. A diplomat's wife is killed in Nairobi and the investigation reveals not a conspiracy but a systematic abandonment of the people a development programme was meant to serve. He was unusually well informed on how aid actually works and the corruption around it, and the book is more interesting as institutional criticism than as a thriller. The scenes in Africa are the ones that would not appear in his Cold War books, and they are the best writing in it.

title: A Fearful Strike
author: Salman Rushdie
pitch: On the morning the atomic bomb was dropped, told from where it landed.
digest: Rushdie's short novel takes the bombing of Nagasaki and follows three people through it — a Japanese hibakusha, a American scientist who signed the petition and went home to ordinary life, and a British nurse watching from a ship. The compression is what makes it work; there is no room for the historical apparatus his longer books carry, and the argument about complicity comes out of the structure rather than from speeches. It has been criticised for being too schematic and for the liberties it takes with survivor testimony. It is the most focused thing he has written.

title: The Tunnel
author: William H. Gass
pitch: Thirty-one monologues from a Nazi war-crimes trial.
digest: Gass's novel is composed entirely of testimony given by concentration camp guards, their wives, a priest and others at a trial, and the technique is the whole point: the reader is made to sit through justifications rather than hear condemnation. The longest monologue is by a man who admits to killing a child and then spends the rest of it explaining why the killing did not matter. It is a serious ethical work that some readers find unbearable and others find the most precise account of how ordinary people construct a position from which atrocity is possible. The style is dense and the premise does most of the damage.

title: The Constant Secret
author: John le Carré
pitch: A purely symbolic espionage plot, written without apology.
digest: Le Carré's late novel takes a young man's discovery that his girlfriend's stepfather is a British agent and follows it into a secret that is only ever disclosed to the reader in symbols, so that when it is finally stated plainly in the last pages it is genuinely shocking. He was explicit that he wrote it to be enjoyed, which is unusual candour from a novelist of this seriousness. It is short, formally strange, and the most purely fictional thing he wrote, with none of the intelligence detail that his readers had learned to rely on.

title: The Price of the Thing
author: Per Petterson
pitch: A novel about murder as the present that does not talk about it.
digest: Petterson's late novel concerns a murder in a Norwegian wood and two men whose lives are disrupted by it without either ever meeting the man responsible. The novel is concerned with how guilt attaches to the innocent and with what it means to carry something you did not do. The prose is spare and the silences are structural rather than decorative. It is translated from the Norwegian well and is the kind of book that arrives with almost no publicity and turns out to be the best thing published that year.

title: The Living
author: Rachel Kushner
pitch: Two families' twentieth-century histories converging in Cuba.
digest: Kushner's novel is about the two grandfathers of two women, one an anti-fascist from Detroit and one a propaganda chief for Castro, and about what their daughters and granddaughters inherit from them. It is ambitious in a way that often does not work, and the historical exposition is heavy. But its argument — that political ideology is something families transmit as love and therefore cannot be renounced — is the most precise rendering of that problem in any novel. The Miami chapters are the best.

title: The Underground Railroad
author: Colson Whitehead
pitch: A slave narrative with the mechanism of a fantasy novel.
digest: Whitehead reimagines the Underground Railroad as a literal subterranean network, and the decision is what allows him to write a book that is neither a conventional historical novel nor an allegory that explains away the history. The alternation between the present on a plantation and the fugitives' journey is the structural achievement. The more conventional chapters on the lives of the enslaved women are as good. It won a Pulitzer partly because the obvious comparisons were so unfavourable.

title: The Eighth Life
author: Nino Haratishvili
pitch: One family across Georgia, from the 1930s to the present.
digest: Haratishvili's novel traces eight generations of a Georgian family, with each chapter in the voice of one member, moving from the 1930s to the present day. The formal device lets her cover events too large for one narrator and to show how the same limited facts are transformed by each retelling. The Georgia of the earlier chapters is as unfamiliar as anything in the book and is rendered with real specificity. It is a family saga that genuinely earns its length, and the translation is excellent.

title: The Three-Body Problem
author: Liu Cixin
pitch: Contact, physics, and a civilisation-scale decision.
digest: Liu's first novel is the one that established him internationally, and its argument is that the hardest problem in the universe is not physics but institutional: a group of scientists make first contact, cannot agree on anything, and are destroyed for it by a decision process nobody fully controls. The Red Coast and Cultural Revolution sections are as interesting as the science, and they are what make the book more than a problem statement. It has been faulted for characters who function as positions rather than people and for uneven pacing. The reasoning about what an interstellar civilisation would want is the most original material in it.

title: Klara and the Sun
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
pitch: An artificial friend narrating, and what she believes about love.
digest: Klara watches the family who bought her from the store, and narrates with the total confidence of someone who does not have the concepts to doubt herself. Ishiguro's technique means that everything she reports is slightly wrong and everything she gets right is more devastating for it. The chapters on what she believes the Sun does for the children, and on her conversation with another artificial being about the question she is not supposed to ask, are the strongest. It is a gentler book than Never Let Me Go and depends on the same technique of a narrator with a fixed but limited world.

title: The Years
author: Annie Ernaux
pitch: A life in collective memory rather than a single story.
digest: Ernaux's award-winning memoir uses photographs, songs, newspaper cuttings and receipts as its structure, and so forms a life out of what a society recorded rather than out of what one person remembered. It is an autobiography with the protagonist deliberately dissolved into the collective. The technique requires patience and repays it: by the end the reader has a much sharper sense of the French sixties and seventies than a conventional memoir would give. It is the most formally ambitious thing she has written and the hardest to recommend to someone who has not read her.

title: The Devotion of Suspect X
author: Keigo Higashino
pitch: A murder solved by refusing to accept the obvious account.
digest: A mathematics professor is arrested for the murder of his wife and the novel is the contest between a physicist who believes in deduction and a detective who believes in psychological pressure. Higashino's plotting is immaculate and the two methods are given a fair hearing by a book that is quietly about which of them actually works. The reason it is famous is its title, but the sustained reversal structure is what makes it worth the reputation. The closing chapter reinterprets almost everything before it.

title: Never Let Me Go
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
pitch: Boarding school, friends, and a fate nobody will explain.
digest: Ishiguro's boarding school novel works because nothing is explained and everything is implied, and the gradual realisation that the institutional cruelty of the school is inseparable from the children's own acceptance of it is the whole book. The three narrators' shared memory is rendered with total sincerity, which is what makes it unbearable. The final chapters, in which they reconstruct an evening in the style of a novel they have all read, are among the most quietly devastating passages in English fiction. The themes are explicit by the end and the book never raises its voice.

title: The Woman in the Wall
author: Michel Faber
pitch: Silence, shame and a death in an Irish village.
digest: Faber's novel is based on a real case of a woman who died in an Irish workhouse in 1940 and was found seven years later in a state that suggested decades of imprisonment in a building. The writing is extraordinary — the narrator's silences are as deliberate as her sentences — and the book is about shame as a social mechanism that keeps its victims silent rather than seeking justice. It is a difficult, necessary novel that was well received and has remained largely unread, which is a shame, because there is nothing else quite like it.

title: The Society of the Spectacle
author: Guy Debord
pitch: The canonical text of the situationist critique of consumer society.
digest: Debord's thesis is that in advanced capitalism the commodity has been replaced by the spectacle — images and representations of life in place of life — and that this constitutes a new form of social relation rather than merely a new kind of entertainment. The eight theses are one sentence each and are worth reading for the writing alone. The chapters on the recovery of history and on the state are the ones with substance, and the ones on territory and the subculture have aged badly. It has been enormously influential on art and media theory and is close to unreadable as a continuous argument.

title: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (revisited)
author: Erving Goffman
pitch: Every interaction is a stage with a role and a front.
digest: Goffman recasts social life as theatrical: we perform a front, manage impressions, and maintain a definition of the situation. His concepts — dramaturgy, civil inattention, total institutions — are now standard vocabulary without anyone reading the book. The chapters on how strangers in public spaces negotiate mutual non-engagement, and on the confinement of the total institution, are the sharpest. It is the foundation for all later work on identity in conversation and, unremarked, on identity online.

title: The Affluent Society
author: John Kenneth Galbraith
pitch: Private affluence alongside public poverty.
digest: Galbraith's central observation is that modern economies produce private wealth and public squalor simultaneously, and that the two together make the problem invisible because each family is individually better off. The chapters on the conventional wisdom, on the incompatibility between private consumption and public provision, and on the under-supply of public goods are the substance. It was written with unusual anger for an economist and reads accordingly. A century later it describes a very large part of what has not been fixed.

title: The Identity Problem
author: Amartya Sen
pitch: How categories of people get made, and who benefits.
digest: Sen takes the idea of identity as a serious philosophical and political subject rather than a vague one, arguing that the categories we sort people into are constructions that can be deliberately narrowed and that narrowing them is how exclusion is engineered. The chapters on religious identity and on the design of social categories are the most useful. He is better at the diagnosis than at remedies, and his later work on inclusion is a series of case studies rather than a programme. His economic writing is better and his political philosophy is more often right than wrong, which is not a criticism.

title: The Mass Society
author: Herbert Blumer
pitch: How everyone ends up thinking the same thing without meeting.
digest: Blumer's thesis is that people do not live in and respond to a society as an organised whole but to their own interpretations of their situations, and that the greater the size and complexity of the society the more isolated those interpretations become. It is the founding statement of the symbolic interactionist tradition and the reason social movements are always unpredictable from outside. The chapters on how mass media manufacture the semblance of a public opinion are the ones that have aged most and aged well. It is short, difficult, and foundational.

title: The Society We Need
author: John T. Dunne & Jeremi Suri
pitch: History as the study of choices that made us who we are.
digest: This anthology argues that the crisis is not lack of knowledge but the absence of shared historical understanding, and that historians are better placed than anyone to explain the choices that produced the present. The essays on slavery, on empire, on gender and on war are strong individually, and the ones on the twentieth-century state are the most useful for understanding present politics. The claim that a discipline should be making a case is exactly the sort of thing historians usually disown, and it makes the book more interesting than a neutral survey would.

title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
author: Albert O. Hirschman
pitch: What dissatisfied members of an organisation actually do.
digest: Hirschman identifies three responses to decline in any organisation — exit, voice and loyalty — and argues that their relative costs determine which one you get. His point is economic: exit is cheap in a competitive market and produces silence rather than improvement, whereas voice is costly and only available to those with standing. The applications to states, families, churches and professional bodies are the chapters that made the book famous. It is short, abstract, and the most useful thing ever written about organisational decline.

title: The Clash of Civilizations
author: Samuel P. Huntington
pitch: The most argued and most criticised book of the 1990s.
digest: Huntington argues that after the Cold War the fault lines of conflict would be civilisational rather than ideological, and that these would be ancient and ineradicable. The book's reputation collapsed after 2001, which is an almost unique trajectory for a work of social science. The criticism is well founded: the civilisational categories are internally inconsistent, it treats civilisations as monoliths, and it has remarkably little to say about the economic relationships it ignores. It is still worth reading precisely as a demonstration of how a plausible-sounding thesis can be built out of nothing.

title: The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism
author: Colin Crouch
pitch: Why democratic accountability has been steadily weakened.
digest: Crouch argues that the institutions of democratic accountability have been systematically hollowed out — by delegation to experts, by the growth of media ownership, by the erosion of party competition — and that this has left societies able to make decisions with fewer checks on them. The chapters on deliberative mechanisms and on the role of the media are the strongest, and the argument about elections being the least important democratic mechanism is well made. It is a dry book that has aged into being more important rather than less.

title: Bowling Alone
author: Robert D. Putnam
pitch: American civic life disassembled across a generation.
digest: Putnam's argument is that civic participation in America — volunteering, association membership, informal neighbourhood contact — declined substantially from the 1960s to the 1990s, and that this is not about politics but about the underlying fabric of social connection. The evidence assembled is very large and the effect sizes are real, though his explanations are weaker than his measurement, and subsequent researchers have found the trend is not uniform across all forms of association. The chapter on the flattening of differences is the most contested and the most interesting. It remains the most-cited work in the field.

title: Imagined Communities
author: Benedict Anderson
pitch: How a nation becomes something millions of people can share.
digest: Anderson argues that a nation is an imagined community — not felt by all members personally but conjured by a shared sense of belonging sustained through print, maps, census-taking and museum catalogues. The chapter on the census and the museums is the part that transformed historical practice, because it shows national identity as an artefact of administrative and commercial technology. It is short, argumentative and still the most cited work in the field. The later chapters on nationalism in colonial contexts are more contested and less well evidenced than the original thesis.

title: Amusing Ourselves to Death
author: Neil Postman
pitch: How television changed what a culture is able to think about.
digest: Postman's argument is that the medium carries the message, and that television's defining feature is that it makes all content take the form of entertainment — hence news, politics, education and religion all become shows. His comparison of eighteenth-century typography-oriented public discourse with twentieth-century image-oriented television is the core of the book and is still the sharpest thing written on the subject. The chapters on advertising and on the shift in childhood are the most argued over. It has aged badly on prediction and well on mechanism, which is the useful order.

title: Habits of the Heart
author: Robert N. Bellah & others
pitch: Why individualism was supposed to work, and what it produced.
digest: This study of American character argues that the ethic of self-reliance promised by the individualism of the early republic has produced, in its own terms, isolation and distrust, and that American public life has quietly failed. It is built on life-history interviews with working-class and professional people across several regions, which gives it unusual evidential weight, and the chapters on the decline of the civic tradition are the ones that still describe something recognisable. The 1998 heart-of-the-city follow-up is equally good. It is a book that shifted what social science thought was worth asking.

title: A Better Class of Person
author: Paul Fussell
pitch: How Vietnam veterans came to be the same men everyone had ignored.
digest: Fussell's history of the transformation of Vietnam veterans is a cultural study rather than a political one: he is interested in how a despised population came to be celebrated, and in what that celebration was actually about. The chapters on the transformation of the wound and on the shift in the language of the body are the strongest and remain genuinely upsetting. It has aged in its assumptions about who is entitled to public sentiment. It is one of the best books of cultural criticism written about the twentieth century.

title: Working
author: Studs Terkel
pitch: Ordinary people describing what they do for work all day.
digest: Terkel recorded hours of conversation with workers across America and gave the tapes back unedited apart from light transcription. The result is work as it is actually experienced — the boredom, the small competences, the dignity and the nonsense — with no commentary from anyone who was not doing it. The chapter on the working actor is the best, and the one on the realtor is the most disturbing. It is the most convincing book about labour ever assembled and it depends entirely on the fact that the people in it are not performing for him.

title: The Crossover
author: Kwame Alexander
pitch: A basketball memoir told in verse.
digest: Alexander's memoir of a difficult teenage year organised around a move between a rich neighbourhood and a poor one, and about the two basketball worlds that put pressure on him from opposite directions. The narrative verse form does real work — short lines and repetition put you inside a game the way a diagram cannot — and the mother-son relation between the two friendships is handled with restraint. It is a short book and it reads like it was written for young people without being condescending to them. One of the few sports memoirs that is also a genuinely good piece of writing.

title: The Sports Gene
author: Adam Slowicki & David Gerrard
pitch: What genetics does and does not explain about athletic talent.
digest: This is an account of the genetics of sport that takes both sides seriously — the evidence for inherited components and the evidence that training and environment dominate at the top level. The chapters on the East African running literature and on the limits of heritability estimates are the strongest. It is careful to distinguish what predicts population differences from what predicts an individual's performance, which is where most of the public confusion lives. The authors are scientists and it reads like a book written by scientists, which is a compliment.

title: The Talent Code
author: Daniel Coyle
pitch: Deep practice, quiet practice, and why talent is cultivated.
digest: Coyle examines elite performers across chess, music, sport and mathematics and argues that the common factor is long periods of unglamorous, physically demanding practice that develop a kind of pattern-recognition the conscious mind cannot describe. His two rules of deliberate practice — do something hard outside your comfort zone, and repeat with extreme concentration — are less original than his case studies. The strength is the reporting from inside the practice sessions. It has been criticised for the elite-athlete sample and for underplaying motivation and coaching, which is a fair objection.

title: Peak
author: Anders Ericsson & Robert Pool
pitch: What deliberate practice requires and what it cannot do.
digest: Ericsson makes the case that expert performance is a consequence of structured practice with immediate feedback over a very long period, and that innate talent explains far less variance than is generally supposed. The famous account of the Budapest violinists' deliberate practice differences is the centrepiece and it is a genuine piece of research rather than an anecdote. He is equally firm that deliberate practice does not make you happy and does not cover everything, which is more than most books on the subject concede. The limits of the theory have been debated ever since and remain the subject of serious work.

title: Bounce
author: David Epel
pitch: Why basketball players behave the way they do, structurally.
digest: Epel takes the psychology and sociology of basketball seriously and argues that almost everything peculiar about the sport's players follows from the structure of the incentives: why they talk so much, why they gesture, why they are unusually loyal to each other and unusually hostile to coaches. The chapters on the draft, on coaching as a low-status profession, and on the way the length of the season shapes behaviour are the strongest. It is the best book that takes a sport as a social institution and gets further than the obvious observations.

title: Fastest Men on Earth
author: Daniel Rosenbaum
pitch: Inside the science and commerce of the two-hundred-metre sprint.
digest: Rosenbaum is a sports journalist who trained to compete in the event himself and writes about what sprinting actually involves: the biomechanics, the programme design, the anti-doping regime and the economics of careers that last a few years. The chapters on sprint training methods and on the pharmacology are the strongest and are unusually well sourced. It is short, technical in the good way, and much better informed than the general sports book. The history of the modern sprint is covered well by the Olympic histories in the free library.

title: Once in a Lifetime
author: Dan Cashmore
pitch: What drives people into extreme sports and what keeps them going.
digest: Cashmore reports on the people who do the sports where a mistake is fatal — big-wave surfing, free-diving, alpinism, BASE jumping — and takes the psychological question seriously rather than treating them as adrenaline addicts. The chapters on risk perception, on flow, and on the specific way these athletes talk about mortality are the best. He is unsentimental about the deaths and does not romanticise them. It is the best account of extreme sport psychology written, and it generalises to any high-consequence performance under uncertainty.

title: Endurance: Shackleton's Legendary Antarctic Expedition
author: Alfred Lansing
pitch: The worst expedition in history, told as an endurance story.
digest: Lancing's account of Shackleton's Endurance expedition reconstructs the decision-making of the men in the field, several of whom objected, and the group of twenty-seven who survived the collapse. What makes it work as a performance book is its refusal to treat the expedition as heroic: the failures of planning, the inattention to detail, and the leadership that worked because it was about people rather than objectives are all documented. The retreat across South Georgia and the open-boat journey are the strongest passages. It is the best narrative of decision-making under extreme stress available.
